lessons.title: Invoices, receipts, and expense papers
lessons.html:
A sales invoice is the bill you give (or send) when you sell goods or services. It lists what was sold and what the buyer should pay. A purchase invoice is the bill you receive when you buy something for the activity you are tracking. A receipt often shows that money was paid. The CRA groups invoices, receipts, contracts, cash-register slips, and other business papers together as records of a sale or purchase.

This is different from the bookkeeping course, which explained day-to-day recording and what a purchase receipt should show for income-tax records. Here the focus is the papers themselves: how to read them, what to put on a bill you send, and how they connect to GST/HST.

A simple habit:

  • Keep sales papers (invoices you send, copies of receipts you give) in one place.
  • Keep purchase and expense papers (invoices and receipts you receive) in another place.
  • Write the date on anything that does not already show one clearly.
  • Do not guess missing numbers.

An estimate or quote is not the same as an invoice. An estimate is a planned price before the work is done. After the work or sale, the invoice (or receipt) is the record of what was actually charged.

The CRA says that if GST/HST applies to a sale, you must let customers know — on a receipt, invoice, contract, or even a posted sign. Lesson 2 explains that wording. This lesson does not tell you whether your activity must charge tax.

Ask your adult learning council if you want help practising a simple invoice layout on paper or in a spreadsheet. This course does not certify any software.

lessons.title: What customers should see about GST/HST
lessons.html:
If GST/HST applies to a sale, the CRA says you must let customers know:

  • that GST/HST is being applied
  • whether the tax is included in the price or added separately

You can do this on cash-register receipts, invoices, contracts, or posted signs.

The CRA also says you have to show:

  • the GST/HST rate that applies to the supply (the sale)
  • the amount paid or payable and the GST/HST amount as separate lines, or a clear statement that the total includes GST/HST

If HST applies, show the total HST rate. Do not split it into a federal part and a provincial part on the invoice.

This course will not tell you which rate to charge. The CRA says the rate depends on where the sale is made (the place of supply) and on the type of supply. Some things are zero-rated (taxed at 0%) or exempt. Use the official CRA pages or a qualified professional for your own sales.

A clear invoice might show a subtotal, a GST or HST line, and a total — or one total with a sentence such as “Price includes GST/HST.” Follow the live CRA wording, not a neighbour’s template from another country (United States sales-tax forms are not Canadian GST/HST records).

If you are not sure whether you must register or charge tax, stop and get official help. Do not invent a rate.

lessons.title: Extra details on invoices of different amounts
lessons.html:
The CRA says suppliers have to put specific information on the invoices, receipts, contracts, or other papers they use when they sell taxable property or services to a buyer who is registered for GST/HST. The buyer needs those details to support official claims. This course will not tell you whether you can claim an input tax credit (ITC) or how to calculate one. It only explains what the CRA chart says should appear, so your papers are complete.

On the CRA page checked in November 2026, the details depend on the total sale:

Every amount (including under $100):

  • the supplier’s business or trading name
  • the invoice date (or, if there is no invoice, the date the GST/HST is paid or payable)
  • the total amount paid or payable

Total sale of $100 to $499.99 — all of the above, plus:

  • the total GST/HST charged, or a note that each taxable amount includes GST/HST at the applicable rate
  • if the invoice mixes taxable and exempt items, an indication of the status of each
  • the supplier’s (or intermediary’s) GST/HST registration number

Total sale of $500 or more — all of the above, plus:

  • the buyer’s name or trading name (or authorized agent)
  • a brief description of the property or services
  • the terms of payment (when and how the buyer should pay)

These dollar amounts can change. Always follow the live CRA chart. They are not the same list as the income-tax receipt details in the bookkeeping course.

Even if you never claim a credit, putting these details on a bill you send helps the buyer and keeps your copy useful.

lessons.title: Checking expense documents and GST/HST numbers
lessons.html:
When you keep purchase invoices and expense receipts, look at them the same day if you can. Ask: does this paper show the name, date, and total? If the amount is $100 or more, does it show GST/HST (or say the price includes it) and a GST/HST registration number? If the amount is $500 or more, does it also name the buyer and describe what was bought?

If something important is missing, ask the supplier for a more complete invoice or receipt while the sale is still easy to remember.

The CRA provides a free GST/HST Registry so you can confirm that a business charging GST/HST is registered. The CRA says this helps make sure official claims include only tax charged by someone who is registered.

To use the Registry you need:

  • the first nine digits of the GST/HST account number (do not type the letters)
  • the supplier’s legal, operating, or trading name
  • the transaction date on the receipt or invoice

The CRA says a supplier must include the GST/HST account number on papers for taxable goods or services of $100 or more. If you cannot find the number, contact the supplier. If the supplier does not provide it, the CRA says you can call the Business enquiries line at 1-800-959-5525 to confirm whether the business is registered.

The CRA suggests printing the Search Details screen if you use the lookup. This course will not tell you whether to claim a credit.

Do not type other people’s GST/HST numbers into this course.

lessons.title: Organizing and storing invoice and GST records
lessons.html:
The CRA says you must keep records that support GST/HST returns and claims. Those records include sales and purchase invoices and other records related to the business and the GST/HST. If someone files electronically, they should also keep working copies of returns. You do not have to send receipts or supporting documents when GST/HST information is filed electronically, but you must keep them in case the CRA asks to see them.

The CRA also says records must let a person calculate the GST/HST collected, the GST/HST paid or payable on eligible purchases and expenses, and any amount to be refunded, rebated, or deducted from net tax. Records should describe goods and services in enough detail to tell whether GST/HST applies. This course will not do those calculations for you or tell you how to file.

Usually, the CRA says to keep records for six years from the end of the year they relate to (page checked November 2026). The CRA may ask you to keep them longer. The bookkeeping course explains the six-year rule and where to store records in Canada in more detail.

A simple filing habit: keep sales papers apart from purchase papers, and keep them in date order — on paper, in folders on a computer, or both. Use any clear system; this course does not require a brand of software.

If you collect GST/HST, the CRA says you hold that money until you send it to the CRA. Ask a professional how that works in your case.
